question:
Patient note:
A 46-year-old man is assessed this morning by the peri-operative medicine service just outside the main operating theatre where the acute care surgery team is preparing for a formal damage-control relaparotomy, washout, and possible diverting ileostomy after a protracted intra-abdominal course that began three weeks ago with an open right hemicolectomy for complicated perforated appendicitis and phlegmon. Since that initial operation he has remained hospitalized, and over the past ten days he has spent the vast majority of each day supine, rising only with assistance to a bedside commode because of abdominal discomfort, low energy, and the presence of two large closed-suction drains that tether him to the bedrails; nursing flow sheets document fewer than 30 feet of ambulation in any 24-hour period. On postoperative day 5 he developed a new fever, purulent sputum, and patchy right-lower-lobe opacities on chest radiograph that were treated empirically with intravenous cefepime and azithromycin; although he defervesced and his leukocytosis resolved, he still produces occasional white sputum and today’s chest examination reveals a few coarse inspiratory crackles at the right base. Because intravenous access had become unreliable after multiple peripheral catheters failed, a right basilic double-lumen peripherally inserted central catheter was placed under ultrasound guidance twelve days ago, flushed this morning with excellent blood return and no local erythema. He denies ever experiencing calf pain, asymmetric leg swelling, or pleuritic chest discomfort suggestive of prior venous thromboembolism, and review of prior imaging finds no duplex ultrasonography or CT pulmonary angiography demonstrating such events. Past medical history is otherwise notable only for a remote episode, five years earlier, in which routine pre-operative laboratory studies for an elective nasal septoplasty revealed an unexpectedly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time; hematology consultation at that time attributed the abnormality to an antiphospholipid antibody pattern rather than factor deficiency, and no anticoagulation was prescribed because he had never clotting manifestations. He carries no diagnoses of chronic lung disease, left-sided heart dysfunction, bowel inflammation, malignancy, or metabolic infarction of the myocardium, and he asserts that his exercise tolerance had been excellent—running five kilometers three times weekly—until the present abdominal catastrophe. He has never required a limb cast, has sustained no orthopedic fractures, has avoided motor-vehicle collisions or other high-energy trauma, and reports no neurologic deficits referable to stroke or spinal cord injury. Medications at the bedside are piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g every six hours, intravenous pantoprazole, and acetaminophen for fever; no antiplatelet, estrogenic, erythropoietic, or steroid agents are prescribed. Socially he never smoked, drinks beer on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Vital signs collected fifteen minutes ago show temperature 37.2 °C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing room air in semi-Fowler position. He lies in bed appearing fatigued but cooperative. Jugular venous contour is not elevated, S1 and S2 are crisp without extra sounds, and peripheral pulses are 2+ symmetric. Auscultation of the lungs discloses scattered coarse breath sounds over the right posterior base with otherwise clear fields. The midline laparotomy wound extends from xiphoid to pubis, is lined with skin staples, and shows no erythema or purulent discharge; two Jackson-Pratt drains exit the left lower quadrant and currently yield cloudy serosanguinous fluid. The abdomen is distended but soft with diffuse tenderness, greatest in the right flank, without rebound or guarding. Both lower extremities are warm, of equal circumference, and free of pitting edema, discoloration, varicosities, or palpable venous cords; passive dorsiflexion and calf compression produce no discomfort. Neurologic screening demonstrates full orientation, intact cranial nerves II–XII, and 5/5 strength proximally and distally, though hip flexion is limited by pain. Laboratory results drawn through the PICC two hours ago reveal hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, platelet count 236 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 7.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, AST 28 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 110 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 44 s—similar to his historical baseline. An electrocardiogram obtained this morning displays normal sinus rhythm at 82 beats/min with no ST-T segment changes, and a supine anteroposterior chest radiograph shows unchanged right basilar patchy infiltrate consistent with his recent lower-lobe infection, intact drain positioning, and PICC tip projecting over the cavoatrial junction. Airway evaluation reveals Mallampati class I with full neck extension; anesthesia foresees routine endotracheal intubation. Sequential pneumatic compression sleeves were prescribed at admission but have remained off for the past two days because the patient reports abdominal discomfort when they tighten; no chemical thromboprophylaxis has yet been given in anticipation of today’s return to the operating room.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score adds perioperative VTE risk factors:
- Age 41–60 years: he is 46 (+1).
- Pneumonia within the past month: postoperative right-lower-lobe pneumonia (+1).
- Major open surgery expected to exceed 45 minutes: planned damage-control relaparotomy (+2).
- Bed confinement for more than 72 hours: 10 days of minimal assisted ambulation (+2).
- Central venous access: indwelling PICC (+2).
- Acquired thrombophilia: documented antiphospholipid antibody pattern (+3). This counts even without prior thrombosis; prior VTE itself scores 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 11.
Final answer: 11
